title: Flows and positioning: what the FII number really tells you
hook:
In October 2024, foreign investors pulled more money out of Indian shares than in any single month in history. Beijing had just announced a burst of stimulus, Chinese stocks were ripping, and fund managers in London and New York were selling expensive India to buy cheap China. Every evening the business channels flashed the foreign selling number in angry red. The phrase of the season was sell India, buy China.

Here's the odd part. Two years earlier, in 2022, foreigners had sold Indian shares at a record pace for a whole calendar year. And the Nifty ended that year slightly higher.

So what do these flow numbers actually tell you? Who are these foreign and domestic institutions, why do they move, and what does it mean when foreigners pile into bearish bets in the futures market? This chapter answers those questions, and along the way it overturns one of the market's favourite bits of folklore: that a crowded foreign short is fuel for a rally. In our data since 2022, it has not been.
short: The daily FII and DII figures are the most quoted and most over-read numbers in Indian markets. Every share sold has a buyer, so the print tells you who was more eager, not where prices go next.

Ownership has shifted. Domestic institutions now own more of listed India than foreigners do, after a decade in which foreign ownership drifted down and monthly SIP money compounded. Persistent foreign selling now meets a structural buyer.

Foreign flows are driven mostly from outside India: US yields, the dollar, emerging-market allocations and India's valuation premium. That is why they can persist through perfectly good domestic data.

In our data since 2022, a crowded foreign short in index futures has not been followed by better-than-normal months, while a crowded long has preceded weaker ones. Foreign bearishness is not rally fuel.
The real risk is a stall in domestic flows. The monthly mutual fund data deserves more of your attention than the daily FII print.

sections.heading: Who these FIIs and DIIs are, and why the daily print misleads
sections.html:
Start with the cast. FIIs, or foreign institutional investors, are officially called foreign portfolio investors these days, but everyone still says FII. They are the giant pools of money from abroad: American mutual funds, Canadian pension funds, sovereign wealth funds from Norway to Singapore, hedge funds, and the exchange-traded funds that mechanically track emerging-market indices. DIIs, domestic institutional investors, are the home team: Indian mutual funds, LIC and the other insurers, pension money from the EPFO and NPS, and banks.

After every trading day, the exchanges publish a provisional figure: how much each group bought and sold in the cash market, and the net. That is the number you see on television.

Here's the thing most viewers miss. Every share sold has a buyer. If foreigners net sold heavily today, someone, usually domestic funds and individuals, bought exactly those shares. Money did not leave the market; ownership changed hands. What the print really tells you is who was more eager. If sellers were desperate and buyers reluctant, prices fell to get the trade done. If domestic buyers were hungry, the same foreign selling might barely dent the index.

Net foreign selling does not mean money left the market. It means foreigners were in a bigger hurry than the people buying from them.

There are more traps.

  • Provisional is not final. The depository's later data can differ, sometimes meaningfully.
  • The cash market is not the whole story. Foreigners also buy shares in IPOs, large share sales by companies and block deals. They can be heavy net sellers on the exchange while putting billions into new issues, a pattern that has been common in recent years.
  • One deal can swing a day. A founder selling a big stake to a foreign fund in a single block can make an ordinary day look like a stampede.

So treat the daily figure as a weather vane, not a forecast. Rolling totals over a month tell you far more, which is why this page tracks twenty-session sums rather than single days.

sections.heading: The quarter domestic money overtook foreign money
sections.html:
For most of the three decades after India opened its stock market to foreigners, foreign money set the direction. When they bought, the market rose; when they sold, it fell, often brutally. Domestic institutions were smaller and, crucially, did not have a steady stream of new money to deploy.

That has changed, slowly and then all at once. A decade ago, foreign investors owned a much larger slice of NSE-listed companies than domestic institutions, by a wide margin. In the March 2025 quarter, according to Prime Database, domestic institutions owned more than foreign investors for the first time since its tracking began in 2009. By September 2025 the gap had widened, with foreign ownership at a thirteen-year low.

Where did all that domestic money come from? Mostly from a habit. The systematic investment plan, or SIP, is a standing instruction to invest a fixed sum in a mutual fund every month, auto-debited from a salary account. Tens of millions of Indians now have one. The industry's long-running campaign telling people that mutual funds were the right choice helped, as did years of steady returns and a pandemic boom in first-time investors. Add the EPFO, which began putting part of workers' provident fund money into equity ETFs in 2015, and the NPS, and you have a giant, monthly, largely price-insensitive buyer.

Why does price-insensitive matter? Because a SIP does not care what the FII print said yesterday. It buys on its appointed date every month whether the market is up or down. When foreigners sell, that money is there to absorb it. That is how 2022 and late 2024 could see record foreign selling without the kind of crash that foreign selling of that size would have caused in 2008.

There is a twist, though. The same domestic money that cushions the falls also keeps Indian valuations high compared with other emerging markets. That premium is one of the reasons global funds have stayed underweight India. The domestic buyer and the foreign seller are, in a sense, two sides of the same coin.

sections.heading: Why foreigners sell even when India is doing fine
sections.html:
It is tempting to read foreign selling as a verdict on India. Mostly, it isn't. Foreign flows are driven largely from outside, by forces an Indian investor has no control over.

Picture a fund manager in Boston running a global emerging-markets fund. Her performance is judged against an index in which India is one country among many, alongside China, Taiwan, Korea and Brazil. Every month she asks four questions, and only one of them is about India.

  • What do US Treasuries pay? When US ten-year yields are high, the world's safest asset offers a handsome return. Every emerging-market bet has to clear a higher bar, and money tends to flow home. This is the single biggest driver.
  • What is the dollar doing? Her returns are measured in dollars. If the rupee falls, her Indian gains shrink even if the Nifty is flat. A strengthening dollar is a double hit: weaker local currencies and a reason to hold cash at home.
  • Where else is cheap? Her money has to go somewhere. When China announced stimulus in September 2024, Chinese stocks suddenly looked like the bargain of the decade, and the money to buy them had to come from somewhere. Expensive India was the obvious source.
  • How expensive is India? Indian shares have long traded at a premium to other emerging markets. When the premium stretches, she trims.

Notice that none of these is India's GDP growth or its corporate earnings. That is why foreign selling can carry on for months through perfectly good domestic data, and why it often stops for reasons that have nothing to do with India either: a fall in US yields, a weaker dollar, a disappointment in China.

Debt flows follow similar logic but matter more for the rupee. Since Indian government bonds began entering global bond indices in 2024, foreign bond money has become a larger swing factor for the currency. The taper tantrum of 2013 showed what happens when it leaves in a hurry.

sections.heading: Reading foreign bets in the futures market
sections.html:
Cash flows tell you what foreigners did. The futures market gives a hint of what they are betting on.

Every day, the NSE publishes who holds open positions in index futures, split into four groups: clients, which are mostly individuals and companies, domestic institutions, foreign investors and proprietary traders. From that, we compute one simple number: of all the index futures contracts foreign investors hold, what share are long bets that the market will rise? The rest are shorts, bets that it will fall.

[[fig:1]]

The top panel shows that long share week by week since 2022, with a dashed line at its median, and the Nifty underneath for context. Notice how wide the swings are, from foreigners being mostly long to being overwhelmingly short, and notice where the line sits at the right edge: deep in the bottom of its range.

Before reading too much into a low number, ask why a foreign fund would be short Nifty futures. There are three very different reasons.

  • Hedging. A fund that owns a large portfolio of Indian shares can protect itself against a fall by selling index futures, without selling a single share. It is faster and cheaper than dumping stocks, and it keeps the portfolio intact. Much of the foreign short is insurance of exactly this kind.
  • Arbitrage. Funds that buy shares and simultaneously sell futures to capture a small price gap show up as shorts too, with no view on direction at all.
  • Outright bearish bets. Some of it really is a view that the market will fall.

You cannot tell from the data which slice is which. That matters a great deal for the folklore we are about to test, because a hedge does not need to be unwound in a panic just because the market ticks up.

sections.heading: Is a crowded short rally fuel? Our data says no
sections.html:
The folklore goes like this. When foreigners are massively short, the market is a coiled spring. Any bit of good news forces them to buy back their shorts in a hurry, the buying pushes prices up, which forces more covering, and you get a short squeeze. So an extremely low long share is a contrarian buy signal.

It is a lovely story. We tested it. We took every trading day since 2022 and sorted them by the foreign long share into three buckets: crowded short, the bottom tail; crowded long, the top tail; and everything in between. Then we measured what the Nifty did over the following twenty sessions, roughly one month.

[[fig:2]]

Read the chart bucket by bucket. Each bar is the average Nifty return over the next twenty sessions, and the label tells you how often the market was up and how many days fell in the bucket.

  • Crowded longs preceded weaker months. When foreigners were most bullish, the Nifty on average fell over the following month and rose less than half the time. Euphoria was a warning, not a confirmation.
  • Normal positioning came with the best average return of the three.
  • Crowded shorts did not precede better-than-normal months. The market did rise more often than not after them, which is why the folklore survives. But the average return was lower than in normal times, not higher. There is no rally premium hiding in there.
When foreigners are heavily short, the market has usually been fine. It has not been better than fine.

Two honest caveats. The twenty-session windows overlap, so a single month-long episode contributes many days; the day counts overstate how much independent evidence there is. And since 2022 covers only a few distinct cycles. This is evidence, not proof.

Why might the folklore fail? Because much of the short is hedging, which does not need covering. And because foreigners are often short for a reason: rising US yields, a strong dollar, an oil shock. When the reason persists, so does the pressure. The practical lesson is to treat a crowded short as context, and a crowded long as the more useful warning.

sections.heading: The risk nobody prices: a domestic flow stall
sections.html:
If the domestic buyer is the cushion, the obvious question is what could deflate it. There are two main threats.

A long, grinding drawdown. A huge share of today's investors arrived after 2020. Many have never sat through a bear market that lasts years rather than months. SIPs are sticky in a sharp, short correction, because people keep paying and buy cheaper units. But a drawdown that drags on long enough to put recent investors' portfolios in the red can test that patience. Investors who stop their SIPs do not make headlines one at a time, but together they can shrink the monthly inflow that has been absorbing foreign selling.

Higher deposit rates. Part of the case for mutual funds over the last few years was that fixed deposits paid little after inflation. When the RBI raises rates, as it did in October 2026, banks eventually lift deposit rates too. A safe, decent return in the bank is real competition for the marginal SIP rupee, especially for cautious savers.

Either of these on its own would slow inflows. Both together, alongside persistent foreign selling, is the scenario in which Indian markets lose the support that has made them so resilient. The flows would stop cancelling out and start pointing the same way.

That is why the monthly mutual fund data from AMFI, the industry body, deserves more attention than the daily FII print. Watch gross SIP inflows, the number of SIPs being stopped compared with new ones started, and net flows into equity funds. Those numbers move slowly, and that is the point: when they turn, they tell you something structural has changed. Our feeds do not carry them yet, so read the monthly release when it comes out.

history_title: who owns India, and who sold it

history.title: The door opens in the year of the scam
history.story:
In April 1992, the journalist Sucheta Dalal exposed how the broker Harshad Mehta had been using money diverted from the banking system to drive stock prices to dizzying heights. The market crashed and the Big Bull became a national scandal.

Months later, in September, India quietly did something far more consequential: following a proposal in Manmohan Singh's budget that year, foreign pension funds, mutual funds and other institutions were allowed to invest in Indian shares. For the next two decades, the money they brought set the direction of the market.
history.lesson: For a generation, the question of where Indian stocks were headed was really a question about foreign flows.

history.title: The minute the market fell off a cliff
history.story:
By 2007, foreign money had powered a spectacular multi-year bull run. Much of it came through participatory notes, instruments that let foreign investors buy Indian exposure without registering with SEBI. In October 2007, SEBI chief M. Damodaran published a paper proposing curbs on them.

The next morning, the Sensex crashed within a minute of the opening bell and trading was halted for an hour. Finance Minister P. Chidambaram rushed to reassure the world that the government was not against foreign investors. Damodaran met investors days later to promise faster registration, and the market bounced back. The rules went through anyway, and were relaxed the following year.
history.lesson: A flow-driven market is hostage to the rules that govern the flow; a hint of a closed door can move it faster than any earnings report.

history.title: The IPO at the top, and the great exit
history.story:
In January 2008, Reliance Power's IPO was the hottest ticket in the country, drawing bids many times the shares on offer from institutions around the world and millions of retail investors. When it listed in February, the shares briefly jumped above the issue price and then closed well below it on day one.

That was the top. Through 2008, as Lehman Brothers collapsed and global funds raced for cash, foreign investors sold Indian shares on a scale not seen since the market opened to them. The market more than halved from its peak. Domestic institutions were simply too small to catch the falling knife.
history.lesson: Flow-driven rallies reverse when the flows do, and without a domestic buyer the drawdowns are brutal.

history.title: When the bond tourists left
history.story:
In May 2013, Fed Chairman Ben Bernanke merely hinted that the Fed might slow its bond buying. Foreign investors who had piled into Indian government bonds for their high yields rushed for the exit. Their selling hit the rupee directly: they sold bonds for rupees, then sold rupees for dollars.

The rupee fell to record lows through the summer, India was branded one of the Fragile Five, and it took a new governor, Raghuram Rajan, and an emergency scheme to attract dollar deposits to turn the tide.
history.lesson: Debt flows matter for the currency as much as equity flows matter for stocks.

history.title: The lockdown generation
history.story:
When Covid shut the country in March 2020, the market crashed. Then something nobody expected happened. Stuck at home, with low interest rates and a phone full of slick broking apps, young Indians opened demat accounts at a pace never seen before. SEBI chairman Ajay Tyagi said in early 2022 that the number of demat accounts had more than doubled since March 2019, and many brokers reported most new customers were under thirty and first-time investors.

Monthly SIP flows climbed alongside. For the first time, Indian markets had a large, growing, domestic buyer that showed up every month.
history.lesson: The domestic buyer arrived, and it changed how Indian markets behave in a sell-off.

history.title: Record selling, and a market that shrugged
history.story:
As the Fed hiked at its fastest pace in decades, foreign investors sold Indian shares at their fastest yearly pace on record, most of it in the first half. In any earlier era, that would have meant a crash.

Instead, domestic institutions invested a record amount, with mutual funds alone pouring in more than twice what they had the year before. The selling was absorbed almost share for share, and the Nifty ended the year slightly higher.
history.lesson: When a structural buyer meets a cyclical seller, the market falls far less than the flows imply.

history.title: Sell India, buy China, and the crossover
history.story:
After Beijing unveiled its stimulus in September 2024, foreign funds rotated hard. October 2024 brought the largest monthly foreign outflow from Indian shares ever recorded, with financials among the biggest casualties. Domestic funds bought through it.

A few months later came the symbolic moment: in the March 2025 quarter, domestic institutions owned more of NSE-listed India than foreign investors for the first time in Prime Database's records.
history.lesson: Foreign selling is now a test of the domestic buyer's stamina, not a verdict on the market's direction.

today:
Over the last twenty sessions, foreign investors have net sold [[val:fii20]] in the cash market, and domestic institutions have net bought [[val:dii20]]. The domestic buyer is absorbing essentially all of it. In futures, the foreign long share is [[val:fii_long]], at [[val:fii_long_pct]] of its range since 2022: heavily short. The Nifty is at [[val:nifty]] and India VIX at [[val:vix]], so for all the selling, the market is not panicking.

The pressure is mostly external: the US ten-year at [[val:us10y]], the oil shock and a defended rupee at [[val:usdinr]]. Do not read the bearish futures positioning as a coiled spring; our data does not support that. Read the monthly fund-flow data instead. The question for the next few months is whether higher deposit rates after the RBI's hike, and a market that has gone nowhere, start to slow SIP inflows.
sowhat:
Foreign selling is heavy and foreign positioning is bearish, but the domestic cushion is holding.

  • Do not bet on a short-covering rally because foreigners are crowded short. In our data, that has not produced better-than-normal months.
  • Be careful with sectors where foreigners own the biggest slice, large financials above all. When foreign funds sell India, they sell what they own most of, as October 2024 showed.
  • Watch the cushion: monthly SIP inflows and stoppages matter more than the daily FII print. A stall there is the real downside risk.
  • Treat a crowded foreign long, when it comes, as a warning rather than a confirmation.

What would flip it: US yields and the dollar easing, the oil shock fading, and foreign cash buying returning together with the long share climbing off its lows. That combination, not a squeeze, is what has historically brought foreigners back.
